meta.title: Uncertainty-Aware Surrogate Modeling of Thrust Vectoring Performance in Differentially Throttled Linear Aerospike Nozzles
meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: Differential throttling enables gimbal-free thrust vector control in linear aerospike nozzles. However, high-fidelity CFD remains prohibitively expensive for iterative design and control. Three uncertainty-aware surrogate models— Gaussian process regression (composite anisotropic RBF + rational quadratic kernel), Support Vector Regression (RBF kernel), and Polynomial Ridge Regression (L2-regularized polynomial expansion)—were trained on steady 2D RANS linear aerospike simulations. The input parameter space (inlet pressure, throttle ratio, ambient pressure) was sampled using two-stage Latin hypercube sampling. Axial and lateral thrust components were predicted independently, with epistemic uncertainty quantified from GPR posterior variance or bootstrapped ensembles (SVR, PRR). Repeated 10-fold cross-validation demonstrates high predictive effectiveness for all surrogates with Gaussian process regression achieving the lowest mean absolute error in both thrust magnitude and thrust vector angle across sparse training sets, while delivering well-calibrated ±3σ bounds with high empirical coverage of test and cross-validation points. The resulting surrogates provide rapid, confidence-aware predictions that bridge high-fidelity aerodynamics and mission-oriented thrust vector control applications.

blocks.html: Aerospike nozzles provide efficient altitude compensation and can allow gimbal-free thrust vector control (TVC) via differential throttling [1, 2]. Although computational fluid dynamics (CFD) accurately predict differentially throttled aerospike flowfields [3], the temporal and computational cost proves prohibitive for rapid design iteration and control applications. Recently, coefficient-based reduced-order modeling (ROM) has demonstrated effective prediction of aerospike cell plume interaction effects at a reduced computational cost [4]. However, this deterministic approach does not address the coupled effects of continuous differential throttling and altitude-driven regime changes, nor does it indicate the model’s confidence, which is critical for mission-oriented aerospike TVC surrogates.

Data-driven surrogates offer a robust, uncertainty-aware alternative. Building on early applications of Kriging for aerospike geometry optimization [5] and recent successes using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) for aerodynamic aleatory uncertainty quantification [6], this paper evaluates the efficacy of GPR, SVR, and PRR surrogates in characterizing the thrust vectoring response of linear aerospikes.

The study utilizes a 2D truncated linear aerospike geometry designed using Angelino’s method [7], as implemented by Silva and Brójo [8]. The truncated linear aerospike contour was designed for a surrogate gas with γ = 1.26, targeting M = 3.0 exhaust. The aerospike contour’s geometric properties are listed in Table 1.

blocks.html: Cold flow (frozen chemistry) steady-state RANS simulations were performed in ANSYS Fluent using the density-based solver and the k −ω SST turbulence model [9]. The fluid domain was discretized using a semi-structured mesh of approximately 3.05 × 105 cells with inflation layer refinement near walls to ensure y+ ≈1. Solutions were iterated sufficiently to ensure the convergence of monitored quantities (thrust component, mass flux), with all residuals below 10−4 and < 0.5% mass imbalance.

Mesh sensitivity was studied by progressively refining the mesh (305k, 520k, 937k). It was found that axial thrust (Tx) and lateral thrust (Ty) varied by 0.8% and 1.6% respectively with the former converging non-monotonically and the latter showing monotonic convergence with apparent order p = 2.17 [10]. While this indicates that discretization is not the sole error source, the low variation between the measured integral quantities (thrust) shows the simulations to be rather mesh insensitive. Therefore, for this study, the coarsest mesh was deemed sufficient.

The dataset was generated by sampling a space of three parameters:

Here pinlet,1 signifies the absolute total pressure at the lower inlet, τ = pinlet,2/pinlet,1 is the throttle ratio (τ = 1 indicating symmetrical throttling) and pamb is the atmospheric (far-field) pressure, applied at the pressure outlet domain boundaries.

The primary inlet pressure was varied over pinlet,1 ∈ [0.56, 4.43] MPa, the throttle ratio over τ ∈[0.5, 1.0], and ambient pressure over pamb ∈[50.5, 202.0] kPa. These bounds span nominal and off-design conditions, enabling analysis of thrust scaling, vectoring authority, and operational limits.

A two-stage Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) [12] strategy was employed to efficiently explore the parameter space while limiting the number of CFD simulations. First, a coarse LHS was generated across the full admissible range to identify degenerate or non-physical regions. Based on these results, a reduced domain corresponding to nondegenerate nominal operation was defined. A second, denser LHS was then applied within this refined region to more precisely characterize the realistic operational region of the nozzle for the purposes of surrogate prediction. Additional LHS points were also placed along refined region boundaries to improve surrogate robustness near operational limits.

Three main surrogate modeling architectures were evaluated and compared: Gaussian Process Regression, Support Vector Regression, and Polynomial Ridge Regression. For all surrogates, separate predictors were trained for the axial (Tx) and lateral (Ty) thrust components and thrust magnitude (|T|) and thrust angle (θ) were computed. The GPR adopted a composite kernel (as recommended by Palar et al. [6]) comprising the sum of an anisotropic RBF kernel (implementing ARD [13] for the three input features) and an isotropic Rational Quadratic kernel. The sum was scaled by a global signal variance and augmented with an additive white-noise kernel. The GPR hyperparameter optimization utilized 10 random restarts to mitigate the non-convexity of the objective function and ensure convergence toward the global maximum.

In contrast, the Support Vector Regression utilized a standard isotropic RBF kernel (as shown optimal for aerodynamic coefficient prediction [14]). To accommodate this isotropic constraint and prevent features with larger numerical ranges from dominating the distance metric, all input dimensions were standardized prior to training using StandardScaler() [15]. The SVR hyperparameters (C, ϵ, γ) were optimized using a cross-validated grid search.

Finally, a Polynomial Ridge Regression was implemented by pairing polynomial feature expansion (degree = [3, 4, 5]) with L2 regularization. Following identical input standardization [15], the polynomial degree and the regularization penalty (α) were optimized via grid search, enabling the model to capture non-linear feature interactions while penalizing over-parameterization.

Feed-forward multilayer perceptron architectures with various hidden layer configurations ([64, 64, 32], [8, 8], [16]) and a linear output layer (Adam, MSE loss) were trained but the resulting predictive accuracy was found to be significantly lower on sparse data (Nmax ≈230). Thus, MLP was excluded from the study.

Thrust magnitude and angle uncertainties were derived via first-order standard uncertainty propagation [16] from the independent Tx and Ty GPR predictions, with the angle uncertainty relying on a small-angle approximation. For PRR and SVR, uncertainty was estimated using a 30iteration bootstrapped Monte Carlo ensemble, training each model on a random 90% data sample to capture variance and mitigate overfitting. The final uncertainty bounds for all surrogates were then defined as ±3σ, quantifying the pointwise confidence across the feature space.

Model performance was assessed using repeated 10-fold cross-validation restricted to the refined (high-fidelity) region. For each training size, five independent resamplings were performed; in each repeat, 20% of refined samples were withheld as an independent test set, while cross-validation folds were constructed exclusively from the remaining refined data. Coarse samples were used for training only and were never included in test sets. Mean absolute errors in thrust magnitude and vector angle were averaged over all folds and repeats, and corresponding standard deviations reported. The withheld 20% set test errors were consistent in magnitude and trend with the crossvalidation errors, showing the robustness of the testing method. Only CV learning curves are therefore included, as they provide a more reliable estimate of expected generalization performance across training sizes, which is the primary focus of this study.

Simulation outputs were verified against idealized thrust coefficients from isentropic relations [11]. The CFD consistently underestimates the ideal thrust coefficient by approximately 22% (Cf/Cf,ideal = 0.785, σ = 4.1 × 10−3), attributed to a high-pressure region spanning roughly 20% of the throat gap upstream of the throat due to sharp inlet curvature. The low variation (σ/µ < 0.6%) indicates consistent bias—suggesting geometric rather than numerical limitations. While thrust performance is suboptimal, the physically consistent results establish a reliable foundation for surrogates and future geometry improvements.

blocks.html: As illustrated in Figure 1, thrust angle scales nearlinearly with τ at sufficiently high NPR, consistent with Hassan et al. [3] and Liu et al. [17]. Predicted angles at τ = 0.70 (≤4.3◦) fall within the 1–4◦range measured by Ruf and McDaniels for an annular aerospike [2], though this comparison is indirect given the geometric differences. At off-design low NPR, the simulations predict flow separation and loss of linearity, consistent with Liu et al., Ruf and McDaniels [2, 17] but diverging from Hassan et al. [3], likely due to differences in turbulence modeling (k−ω SST [9] vs. S.A. [18]). Direct experimental validation remains necessary before hardware-level performance claims can be made.

blocks.title: Surrogate Predictive Accuracy and Learning Curves

blocks.html: The scaling of CV predictive error for GPR, SVR, and PRR is shown in Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4 respectively. At N = 160, GPR achieved a MAE of 10.7 ± 5.9 [N] and 0.01±0.01 [◦], compared to 15.0±6.0 [N] and 0.02±0.02 [◦] for SVR and 27.1 ± 15.5 [N] and 0.11 ± 0.07 [◦] for PRR, compared to the average thrust magnitude of ≈30300 [N] and thrust angle between 0 to 7.5 [◦] in the refined region. The MAE of the surrogates are comparable to the CFD discretization uncertainty, suggesting that the models approach the noise floor, possibly as early as N = 80 for GPR (Figure 2a). However, the 3σ confidence interval narrows with additional data.

At N = 160, the 3σ predictive uncertainty averaged over 1000 randomly chosen points in the operating region was 59.8 [N] and 0.061 [◦] for GPR, 72.8 [N] and 0.21 [◦] for SVR, and 154.8 [N] and 0.48 [◦] for PRR. The GPR surrogate’s ±3σ uncertainty band encompassed 98.8% and 98.4% of all thrust magnitude and thrust angle CV-test points respectively. SVR covered 97.22% and 100%, and PRR covered 96.65% and 96.24%. The high empirical coverage combined with low predictive variance indicates wellcalibrated uncertainty with mild under-coverage (expected 99.7%) within the operational region. All three models significantly outperformed linear interpolation in MAE, exhibited lower MAE variance (indicating robustness), and showed 4-12 times narrower 3σ intervals.

blocks.html: SVR incurs the longest training time because it trains an ensemble of 60 models (30 Tx and 30 Ty), followed closely by GPR owing to automatic relevance determination (ARD) and 10 restart hyperparameter optimization. However, because the inference of bootstrapped models requires 60 evaluations, GPR achieved 5.4 times faster inference than SVR. The dominant computational cost for each surrogate is the generation of the training data set, thus it can be argued that GPR is the most computationally efficient as it achieves any given MAE threshold with the least number of samples (N) with SVR close behind. Its advantage is particularly prominent with low sample counts as both SVR and GPR appear to hit the CFD data noise floor within N = 160. The average wall time of a single simulation on four cores of the HPCC Wildly cluster [19] was approximately 4 hours, meaning the surrogate reduces the marginal per-query inference cost by a factor of 7.6 × 108, 1.4×108, and 9.1×108 for GPR, SVR, and PRR respectively.

The study demonstrated that the investigated shallow learning based surrogate architectures are able to make rapid and accurate interpolative predictions of the thrust vectoring performance of truncated linear aerospikes, with composite kernel GPR showing the best predictive performance and computational efficiency for N ∈[20, 160], followed closely by RBF SVR (aligning with the findings of Palar et al. [6]) though it remains to be investigated how the effectiveness of SVR and GPR varies with aerospike geometry, input dimensionality, and operating ranges. This is relevant because it bridges the gap between computationally expensive supersonic CFD and applications requiring multiple rapid evaluations such as iterative procedural nozzle design and simulated control testing.

The method’s strength lies in its high accuracy with sparse data and well-calibrated epistemic uncertainty quantification which indicates the confidence of the model in each mean prediction. The resulting confidence interval can facilitate responsible stochastic modeling of systems and Monte-Carlo analyses, for example with uncertainty represented as bounded stochastic noise within 6-DOF flight dynamics simulations. Furthermore, future work can use this uncertainty as guidance for adaptive sampling, potentially further improving data efficiency.

However, the limitations must also be understood. Steady-state 2D RANS omits transient effects critical for control (hysteresis, instability). Current UQ is purely epistemic from the surrogate; future applications must account for turbulence modeling error and end-wall losses (validation with experiments/3D CFD). Extension to higher dimensional input (coflows, geometry [5]) and its effects on the required number of training samples must also be investigated. While significant physical modeling challenges remain, these results suggest that uncertainty-aware surrogates offer a viable pathway for streamlining the characterization of linear aerospike TVC, providing a more responsible foundation for the early-stage performance evaluation and simulated testing.
